{{short description|Brazilian doctor, immunologist and parasitologist}}
{{Expand German|topic=bio|date=March 2016}}

'''Ruth Sonntag Nussenzweig''' (20 June 1928 – 1 April 2018<ref name="FSP">{{cite web |url=https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/ciencia/2018/04/ruth-nussenzweig-precursora-no-estudo-da-vacina-contra-a-malaria-morre-aos-89.shtml |title=Ruth Nussenzweig, precursora no estudo da vacina contra a malária, morre aos 89 |date=2018-04-02 |work=[[Folha de São Paulo]] |access-date=2018-04-03}}</ref>) was an Austrian-Brazilian immunologist specializing in the development of [[malaria vaccine]]s. In a career spanning over 60 years, she was primarily affiliated with [[New York University]] (NYU). She served as C.V. Starr Professor of Medical and Molecular [[Parasitology]] at [[Langone Medical Center]], [[Professor#Research professor|research professor]] at the NYU Department of Pathology, and finally professor emerita of [[Microbiology]] and [[Pathology]] at the NYU Department of Microbiology.<ref name="nyu_bio">{{cite web|title=Ruth S. Nussenzweig|url=https://med.nyu.edu/faculty/ruth-s-nussenzweig|website=NYU Langone Health|access-date=11 October 2017|language=en}}</ref>

==Biography==
Nussenzweig was born Ruth Sonntag in [[Vienna]], [[Austria]], to a secular Jewish family in which both of her parents were physicians.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Genzlinger|first1=Neil|title=Ruth Nussenzweig, Who Pursued Malaria Vaccine, Dies at 89|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/04/11/obituaries/ruth-nussenzweig-who-pursued-malaria-vaccine-dies-at-89.html|access-date=16 April 2018|work=The New York Times|date=12 April 2018|page=A29}}</ref> In 1939, after the [[Anschluss]], the Sonntags fled to [[São Paulo]], [[Brazil]]. While attending the [[University of São Paulo]] School of Medicine, she became involved in leftist politics and met Victor Nussenzweig, her future husband and lifelong research partner.<ref name="Science">{{cite web |author=Catanzaro, Michele |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/fresh-start-back-brazil-85 |title=A Fresh Start, Back in Brazil, at 85 |work=Science |access-date=2018-04-03}}</ref> After receiving her [[Doctor of Medicine|M.D.]], Nussenzweig moved to Paris for a research fellowship. In 1963, she did further graduate work at the NYU laboratory of immunologist [[Zoltán Óváry]].

In 1965, the Nussenzweigs returned to São Paulo, and found that working conditions had become untenable since the [[1964 Brazilian coup d'état|1964 military coup]]; many of their friends and colleagues had been jailed by the regime, and Victor was singled out for questioning by the school's new military administration. Through the intervention of [[Baruj Benacerraf]], both Nussenzweigs obtained [[assistant professor]]ships at NYU, and moved permanently to the United States. Nussenzweig returned briefly to Brazil to defend her doctoral thesis, earning her [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the University of São Paulo in 1968.<ref name="Science"/>

Nussenzweig's family includes multiple people who have made significant contributions to research and academia, including husband Victor, professor emeritus at the NYU School of Medicine; son [[Michel C. Nussenzweig]], professor of medicine at The [[Rockefeller University]]; daughter Sonia Nussenzweig-Hotimsky, professor of anthropology at the Foundation School of Sociology and Politics in São Paulo; and son Andre Nussenzweig, Distinguished Investigator at the [[National Institutes of Health]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/fresh-start-back-brazil-85|title=A Fresh Start, Back in Brazil, at 85|date=2013-06-25|newspaper=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=2017-02-14}}</ref>

==Research work==
In 1967, Nussenzweig demonstrated that mice could acquire immunity to the ''[[Plasmodium berghei]]'' parasite. She did so by exposing the mice to ''P. berghei'' [[sporozoites]] that had been inactivated by [[X-ray]] [[irradiation]].<ref>{{cite journal | last = Nussenzweig | first = Ruth | authorlink = Ruth Nussenzweig | author2 = J. Vanderberg | author3 = H. Most  | author4 = C. Orton | title = Protective Immunity produced by the Injection of X-irradiated Sporozoites of Plasmodium berghei | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 216 | pages = 160–162 | date = 14 October 1967 | url = http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v216/n5111/Antibodies/216160a0.html | doi = 10.1038/216160a0 | access-date = 2016-03-03 | issue=5111 | pmid=6057225| bibcode = 1967Natur.216..160N | s2cid = 4283134 | url-access = subscription }}</ref>
